ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Repeat interval is 30 days against a 1h (Anthropic) or 24h (OpenAI) max TTL, so provider carryover across runs is exactly zero — the reuse layer competes against full tuned price, not against a discount. On an unchanged contract it eliminates the call entirely (100% of input AND output), where the tuned baseline still pays ~29% of input plus 100% of output. Two further slices the provider cannot reach at all: the 8,670 deterministic tool ops (OCR at $0.01-0.05/page is comparable to the whole LLM bill and is 100% redundant on a re-scan), and cross-tenant identity on public/vendored documents.
ranked.why: Best combination in the set: executed agreements are immutable artifacts (96-97% byte-identical month to month), the graph is 510 genuinely independent 34-op subgraphs under a 27-op reduce tail with no whole-corpus root, and the cadence is far outside every TTL. Critically, sharding the playbook into 12 per-clause-group artifacts keeps ~11/12 of the extraction layer alive even on the playbook-edit re-runs that trigger roughly half of all re-scans — that one structural choice is worth more than everything else in the workload.
ranked.risk: Downgraded from the spec's implied ~90% for three reasons the critiques found: the graph specifies a retrieval pipeline while the baseline specifies full-document caching (two different workloads being compared), the baseline arithmetic is wrong (77% should be ~71%, and 1h writes are 2x not 1.25x), and the Batch API is missing entirely — a monthly latency-insensitive portfolio scan is the canonical 50%-off job, which halves the pot. The single unmeasured killer is DMS re-export churn: the spec asserts 10-40% of documents get new file IDs for byte-identical content, but a re-OCR or re-render produces *different* bytes, and if even a third of that churn is byte-changing, reuse falls from ~96% to ~70%.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: The 2,496 pairwise sufficiency-judge ops are 63% of run cost and each carries ~2,758 uncached tokens plus 350 output tokens that no prefix cache discounts; skipping the call takes all of it. The frozen control root (312 ops reading zero tenant data) plus the 68 vendor SOC 2 PDFs — the same documents for every tenant using Datadog — are cross-tenant identical, which provider caches structurally cannot serve because they are org/workspace-isolated by design.
ranked.why: The cleanest two-root structure in the set: one root is frozen by construction (control catalogue, zero tenant data, byte-identical across every night and every tenant) and one churns (~15% of evidence artifacts nightly), meeting at a wide pairwise fan-out with no cross-op coupling. Roughly 83% of the money layer is bit-identical night to night, and changes cluster in three control families rather than spreading uniformly.
ranked.risk: Everything hinges on one keying decision the stated transitive rule gets WRONG: index_build is a 744-way global reduction, so under strict transitive keying a 0.3% input change invalidates 100% of the judge layer — 83% reuse or 3% reuse, decided by whether the judge keys pairwise on (control_assertions_hash, evidence_card_hash) or on the retrieval op's output hash. Pairwise keying is also a deliberate soundness weakening: a new artifact that should have displaced a stale one from the top-8 is never judged. Further haircuts: Batch API omitted (baseline $66 should be ~$33), the 18% posture-blob churn supplying 32 of 55 changed artifacts is a pure estimate, rubric churn during the first two quarters of a deployment may run weekly and zero the whole store, and the spec's own threat 5 shows reuse turns the second breakpoint from 7-reads-per-write into a net loss on incremental runs.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: 411 of 419 model ops sit in one flat account-scoped band; the tuned prefix cache discounts the shared 14K policy spine to 0.1x but still pays full freight on each account's GL slice, prior workpaper, subledger extract, and all 216K output tokens. Serving a dormant account's whole operation removes all of it. But note the exposure: intra-close re-runs are 40 minutes to 4 hours apart, which sits INSIDE OpenAI's zero-premium 24h tier — this is the scenario where a provider TTL extension eats the moat outright.
ranked.why: Structurally the most reuse-friendly shape available: one embarrassingly-parallel band with only 32 explicit intra-band edges, between a narrow root and an 8-op apex, re-run ~7 times per close against state where only 8-30 of 420 account shards move between passes. It is also the only spec that builds the free incumbent (BlackLine-style auto-certification clearing 58% of accounts and 93% of JEs) into the graph as a layer rather than arguing it in prose, and its grader is the best reuse instrument in the set — reuse_efficiency, false_reuse_count and wasted_recompute computed against a known oracle closure.
ranked.risk: The `sourced: true` flag is mislabeled: the headline blends two numbers the spec's own basis calls estimated, and the ~7 intra-close re-runs is explicitly named 'the single weakest load-bearing number' — if it is really 2, the blended change rate roughly triples and this drops several places. The L0_5_shred is a prerequisite, not an optimization: without it, one posted journal entry invalidates all 419 model ops and measured reuse is exactly zero. Non-hermetic ERP exports (row order, header timestamps, locale decimal formatting) drive reuse_efficiency to ~0 while every correctness metric stays green — a silent failure. And the absolute prize is ~$335/yr for the modelled customer; the economics only close on the CAS/BPO axis at 40+ tenants sharing a firm-owned policy spine.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Output tokens are 68% of the residual after tuning ($5.72 of $8.38) — the highest output share in the set — and prefix caching discounts none of it. The requisition-independent extraction layer (llm_normalize_resume, keyed only on resume bytes + model id) is also invisible to the customer's existing candidate×requisition score table, so cross-requisition and silver-medalist re-screens are genuinely incremental.
ranked.why: Resume artifacts have a 0% mutation rate as a structural property of every ATS — a corrected resume is a new attachment with a new id, never an in-place edit — so pool change is purely additive at ~9%/week. That is a materially easier problem than code, where the same file is edited in place run after run and keys break at the root constantly. The graph is 200 independent chains with a tiny shared root.
ranked.risk: The incumbent owns the high-frequency path: every production screener already has a candidate_requisition_score row keyed on (candidate, req, rubric_version, model_version), so the reuse layer's honest claim is only finer-than-candidate granularity plus cross-req extraction sharing. Rubric edits invalidate the whole scoring layer on ~40% of re-runs and model bumps (estimated ~2/month, though a regulated LL144-audited product plausibly bumps quarterly) zero all 665 model ops. Provider-optimal and reuse-optimal structures are in direct conflict here — making group_b a continuation turn maximizes caching but couples the two reuse keys. Batch API also omitted from the baseline.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Annual-to-biennial cadence is beyond every provider mechanism including OpenAI's 24h tier and Google's rented explicit cache (holding 1M tokens for a year is absurd at $0.50-4.50/MTok/hour). Provider carryover across runs is structurally, permanently zero, and the 8,200-op screening layer is 94% pure single-record functions whose entire cost — uncached suffix plus output — disappears on a hit.
ranked.why: The most favorable dependency shape on paper: 8,200 mutually independent leaves each reading one record plus a frozen criteria block, no cross-record coupling, and a regulatory requirement that pushes rigorous customers toward undated full re-searches (which is precisely the workflow reuse accelerates) rather than the free date-limited update search.
ranked.risk: Two arithmetic corrections drop it: the layer table sums to 13,874 ops not 9,774 (record_project's 4,100 omitted), so the wide layer is 59% of ops not the claimed 94%. The baseline is fixed at batch=1 on an unsourced sensitivity claim, excluding a ~30% free saving and inflating the denominator. Dedup as implemented is one op emitting one library — a single new record then invalidates all 8,200 screening ops, so the store requires the customer to shard it per-record. Criteria amendments (2-6 during a review's build phase) invalidate 100% with no partial credit, and are exactly what triggers a re-run. Worst structural tension: a 12-month gap against a 12-18 month model deprecation cycle means the runs with the largest prize are the ones most likely to straddle a forced model change that zeroes the key. Prize is ~$60/run, ~$18k/yr at 300 device families.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Output is 64% of the tuned per-call cost — prefix caching removes 66% of input and zero output, so the residual it cannot touch is the majority of the bill. The translate op is also one of the cleanest pure functions in any of the 24 workloads: fully determined by (segment, key path, description, constraints, locale, glossary slice, style guide, model, decode params), with no clock, filesystem, or ordering dependency, so the transitive key composes with no fudging.
ranked.why: Best-measured change rate in the entire set — 88 consecutive release-pair diffs plus 133 time-windowed snapshots across three real shipped catalogs, with the two mature catalogs independently agreeing (median 0.28% vs 0.18% per release). Wide-independent, 30 locale pipelines with zero cross-locale edges, and cadence far beyond any TTL.
ranked.risk: Translation memory is a thirty-year-old, free, content-addressed, cross-project incumbent that already does exactly the leaf-level thing being proposed; the marginal claim collapses to 'TM keys on the source segment alone and will happily serve a hit when the glossary, key path or length constraint changed.' Batching is the decider and points the wrong way: at batch=25, 1.1% key churn becomes 24.1% operation invalidation (22x amplification), and at batch=1 you give back the prefix amortization the baseline depends on. The spec's claim that 42% duplicate values give a 30-40% cold-run internal hit rate is invalid at batch=25 — the key includes 25 distinct key paths. Steady-state incremental runs are ~170 calls costing single-digit dollars; the money is in full passes, which have no prior run except cross-tenant, and cross-tenant leaks unreleased product copy.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: The two mechanisms are close to orthogonal here, which is rare: prefix caching removes ~49% by discounting the shared preamble, but what survives is the per-product supplier record, spec text and page IMAGES (the largest token line in the vision layers) plus all output tokens — unique per product by construction and permanently unreachable by any prefix mechanism. A reuse hit skips the images too.
ranked.why: 20,000 independent shallow chains over a handful of shared roots, so invalidation is naturally surgical (one changed supplier record touches 19 of 380,800 ops). Cost is top-loaded in vision attribute extraction while prompt churn is bottom-loaded in copy/SEO/translation, so the most common invalidation event (a copy-tuning prompt edit, ~45% of full re-runs) preserves the most expensive layers.
ranked.risk: The headline '60% expected, 0% on 17% of runs' rests entirely on an unsourced trigger distribution, and the structure is anti-correlated in the worst way: full re-runs happen almost exclusively BECAUSE a root changed, so hit rate is lowest precisely when spend is highest. The baseline omits per-call packing on 140,000 of 260,800 model ops (3 alt texts and 4 locales per product obviously belong in one call), which hands the reuse layer credit a batching loop gets for free. Model tiering does not reconcile with the stated $0.1363/product, so the '~40% of dollars at L4' premise for the top-loaded argument does not follow. The shared ANN dedupe index is a cross-product coupling that under transitive keying is dirty every run and is never traced. Customer content-hash delta gate already exists.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: 24h repeat interval against a 1h TTL means every nightly run starts stone cold on Anthropic; ~6,000 of 7,890 evidence-extraction calls are skippable outright, taking both the ~1,000 uncached input and the 350 output tokens where prefix caching saves neither.
ranked.why: The strongest premise in the set is regulatory rather than statistical: CMS/AHIMA amendment guidance requires the original entry remain retrievable, so signed clinical notes are byte-identical tomorrow BY LAW — corrections arrive as addenda, never in-place edits. ~72% of documents a nightly run reads it already read last night. The grader is also the best-grounded (real free CMS grouper, MCE tables, and net signed dollar bias to catch systematic upcoding).
ranked.risk: The funnel ops are definitionally whole-encounter — L5 principal-dx selection, L7 grouping, L10 rationale each consume the full encounter, and ~80% of the census gains at least one note nightly, so 42% of model ops and the highest-value decisions recompute unconditionally. Two switches could zero it entirely and neither is verified: per-run randomized HIPAA safe-harbor surrogate names/dates change every document hash every run with no error surfaced, and discharge-only coding (rather than concurrent nightly review) has essentially no cross-run surface at all. The 54% copy-forward redundancy is invisible to document-level hashing, and harvesting it at block level degrades the POA and clinical-significance judgments being sold. Baseline is already ~$0.35/encounter with Batch.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Nightly cadence, 24h apart, so provider carryover is exactly zero; and the mechanism is not action caching at all but Bazel-style EARLY CUTOFF — L6_profile must always re-execute (raw input changed) but L7's tolerance-banded output is byte-identical on a healthy table-night, so the downstream model call's key never moves. No provider mechanism expresses that.
ranked.why: The only spec that correctly identifies early cutoff as distinct from key-hit reuse, and the domain fits it: the query is perfectly stable (the same contract question every night) while the evidence is 100% fresh, which is exactly the configuration where banding a deterministic tool output rescues the expensive layer above it.
ranked.risk: The likely dominant competitor is missing from the baseline entirely: L7 already emits banded verdicts and L8 emits PASS/FAIL, so a competent team gates the semantic_check on non-nominal signal and never issues the call — under that arm the 34-37 'reused' L9 calls were never made, and most of the claimed 50-58% evaporates. The 85-92% table-night banded-stability figure that produces the whole estimate is admitted to be unmeasured. The reuse key can cost more than the operation: content-hashing a 10^8-row table means a full scan at $1-5 against a $1.75 run, unless the customer is on Iceberg/Delta where snapshot IDs are free. And reusing an observation of live state (schema snapshot, profile, check run) is a validation bypass — the ops with the highest naive hit rate are exactly the ones whose purpose is to be re-executed.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Output is 47% of this run's bill and is undiscounted in both arms. The per-PR arm is the real story and is unreachable by any provider mechanism: each of ~40 daily PR branches differs from the main commit the nightly already processed by ~9 files (0.2% of artifacts), so a full-corpus check that costs 4 minutes becomes ~10 seconds — a capability change (engineers stop disabling the check) rather than a discount.
ranked.why: Two independent wings converging on a wide adjudication layer, changes land purely at leaves, and the cadence structure is unusually good: the nightly establishes the store and 40 PR runs per day harvest it against a near-identical corpus. 57% of ops are deterministic tool work that caches for wall-clock even when it saves no dollars.
ranked.risk: The nightly path is badly amplified by a measured correlation the analyst found only after measuring it (and revised upward 2x→6x): files with the most documentation churn at 2.1x repo average, because teams document what they are actively building, and doc fan-in is heavy-tailed to 84 pages for one file. Baseline arithmetic applies an input-side multiplier to total cost (0.46x should be ~0.71x). The grader vendors a REAL repo, so pre-existing doc staleness contaminates a hard precision≥0.90 gate and can fail a correct run. Graph specifies 1,200 adjudicate ops while the baseline batches 4 sections into 300 calls — two different workloads, and the batching/reuse tension is never flagged. `git diff --name-only HEAD@{1}` piped into a file skip is the free competitor.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: 24h between nightly sweeps means the 9k campaign prefix is always cold at run start regardless of tuning. The prize the provider cannot touch is the per-file variable suffix (~2.2k triage / ~3.5k edit at full rate), all output tokens, and the 3x attempt multiplier — non-determinism forces three independent edit attempts per file, and the reuse key pins sampling params and attempt index, so an unchanged file's three attempts collapse to three store hits.
ranked.why: Narrow root, genuinely independent wide middle (168 of 234 model ops), total-fan-in tail that costs zero tokens. ~87% of candidate files are byte-identical night to night over a 5-20 night campaign, and the triage layer is pure repeated negative work: index expansion to distance-5 is deliberately over-inclusive, so ~64 of 90 candidates get 'no change needed' re-derived every night for the campaign's life.
ranked.risk: The spec's own threat 1 is decisive and honest: `rg old_symbol` costs nothing and a 20-line JSON sidecar keyed on (file sha, spec sha) captures an estimated 70-80% of the prize, so the general store must beat THAT and its marginal value is 20-30% of a prize measured in cents per night. A Claude-Code-style single-conversation harness linearizes the DAG so op N's inputs include the whole transcript and reuse degenerates to all-or-nothing — the DAG only exists with a Google-style stateless per-file orchestrator most customers do not have. Root spec revision after review happens in most campaigns and lands on the highest-spend runs. The grader's replay explicitly excludes commits touching the target symbol, so a stale hit can never be scored wrong.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: L8 canonical-copy generation is ~40% of output tokens and is a pure function of the golden record; L2 extraction is 34% of spend and depends only on projected free text. Both carry per-listing content the prefix cache cannot amortize plus output it cannot discount. Cross-tenant identity on open marketplace/dealer/catalogue listings is also structurally unavailable to org-isolated provider caches.
ranked.why: The only genuinely relational dependency shape among the 24 — deterministic blocking, a GBDT scorer, LLM escalation on only the ~11% gray band, union-find, then a global stitch — which makes it the right instrument for testing whether transitive keying survives pairwise coupling rather than clean fan-out. ~97.5% of listings are semantically identical night to night once the projection strips volatile fields.
ranked.risk: Two amplifiers and one poison node. 512 blocking shards at 15.6 listings each turn 2.5% listing churn into 33% shard invalidation (13x), and L6b's fan-in of 512 invalidates with probability ~1.0 every run, poisoning 6,790 model ops — 42% of model ops and ~55% of token spend — unless consumers can key on a SLICE of an upstream output rather than its whole hash. Feed hygiene is binary: raw-record bytes differ ~9%/day on a good RESO delta feed and ~100%/day on PMS full-snapshot exports, so naive keying yields near-zero on a meaningful fraction of customers and getting to 97.5% requires per-customer projection engineering, not a drop-in. The hand-rolled hash(remark_text + prompt_version) memo table already owns L2 and L8 (~75% of the theoretical saving), and MLS licensing plausibly forbids the cross-tenant multiplier outright.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: 24h cadence versus 1h TTL, so the 15.2k shared prefix is written cold every single night. The largest clean win is not tokens at all: 860 pytest/coverage executions (~15 of the 35-45 minutes) are pure re-execution over unchanged inputs, and prefix caching cannot touch a tool op. Repairs are already ~90% discounted by keeping them in the same conversation, so the reuse layer gets almost nothing extra there.
ranked.why: Wide layered DAG of 340 independent per-target subtrees; acceptance is lossy (Meta: 75% build, 57% pass, only 25% raise coverage), so ~4 of 5 targets attempted last night are still uncovered tonight and get attempted again against a repo that moved ~4%.
ranked.risk: As shipped, generate_tests transitively depends on one coverage_parse over one whole-repo coverage.xml, whose key changes every night without exception — reuse is EXACTLY zero, and the fix (1,200 per-file keyed slices) is a customer pipeline rewrite no drop-in layer can perform. Lockfile bumps 2-5x/week invalidate all 860 execution-layer ops at once, erasing the strongest win on those nights, and keying on less than the lockfile means eventually serving a cached PASS for a test the current dependency set fails. `git diff` file-skip captures most of the rest for free. Negative caching is unresolved: max_iterations exists because resampling IS the repair mechanism, so caching three failures makes a target permanently unrecoverable.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Nightly runs are 24h apart and the max TTL is 1h, so provider carryover between runs is exactly zero — everything the reuse layer wins here is win the provider structurally cannot offer. A secondary and arguably larger benefit is report stability: a resource nobody touched currently flips between 'benign' and 'security-relevant' from sampling variance, producing phantom Jira churn, and serving from the store fixes that by construction.
ranked.why: Wide base of 40 independent workspace pipelines, ~98.4% of resource observations semantically identical night to night after canonicalization, and ~93-95% of leaf-level model ops (drift_triage, finding_triage) would hit a cross-run store.
ranked.risk: The ~380-entry volatile-attribute denylist, not the cache, is the load-bearing engineering — it produces the entire 6x gap between the 9.5% raw and 1.6% semantic change rate, it is hand-maintained per provider per resource type, and suppressing one field too many builds a system that reliably hides a real change. Four single points of total invalidation (Checkov pack weekly, provider pin monthly, system preamble whenever anyone iterates, model id) drag realized hit rate to ~70-80%. The baseline cost model double-counts the discount and understates tuned dollars ~3.5x, so the residual is larger than stated but the absolute prize is still ~$1.2k/yr for the modelled fleet. And SOC 2/CIS is an explicit demand that every resource be evaluated on a cadence — 'we served last night's verdict because the bytes matched' is an awkward audit conversation, and shadow-verifying it to a 1%/95% bound costs ~299 recomputes per class per window, which at this hit volume approaches recomputing everything.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Whole-service skip removes ~22k of model input AND 1-4 minutes of build/test compute per untouched service — the provider cache discounts the shared 15k prefix but you still pay full rate on the 7k of per-service content and full compute on the build. The genuinely uncontested slice is cross-tenant root sharing: the migration brief and API diff for a public module pair are byte-identical for every customer on earth bumping that pair, computed from public artifacts with no privacy exposure, which org-isolated provider caches can never serve.
ranked.why: 60 near-independent per-service chains under a shared root; on a nightly campaign re-run the root is byte-identical for the full 2-6 week campaign and 20-40% of services had zero commits overnight, making their entire subgraph skippable wholesale.
ranked.risk: svc_build reads ~410 files per service and svc_test reads more, so a measured 2% FILE-level change produces 60-80% SERVICE-level invalidation of exactly the ops that cost the most compute — fixing it means teaching the layer the build system's own dependency graph, at which point you have rebuilt Bazel for customers who mostly already have it. The next-version sweep (the second most common repeat mode) changes one version string and invalidates all 1,229 downstream keys despite 95%+ of source being identical. Impure ops (lock regen, dep resolve read the live registry) are either unsound or unhittable. repair_patch is 44% of input tokens and arguably must not be cached, since teams specifically want a fresh attempt after a failure. The 20-40% zero-commit figure is the whole case and is unmeasured; the grader's uniform-random churn model destroys it before the domain gets a chance to.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: fix_generate is the one genuine gap: its 9,000-token full-file block is per-file, so prefix caching amortizes it only across 1.6 retry attempts, while a key on (file content, rule, verdict) reuses it perfectly across runs — and it is the largest token layer in the graph. Nightly/weekly cadence also means the provider cache contributes exactly zero across runs; its entire benefit is intra-run across the concurrent triage calls.
ranked.why: 5,100 of 5,166 ops are per-finding leaves reading 1-3 files each, and at ~0.9%/day file churn (concentrated: 2.4-9.9% of files carry 50% of touches) ~97% are byte-identical between nightly runs. Cross-tenant sharing on vendored dependencies and framework-idiom false positives is real — the same log4j 2.14.1 is triaged independently in 400 customer repos today.
ranked.risk: The domain already ships a free, exact version of this: GitHub code scanning matches results across runs via SARIF partialFingerprints, Semgrep persists triage state, and Semgrep Assistant autotriages NEW findings only, capped at 10 per diff scan. The warm production graph is 5-50 model ops, not the 1,602-op cold graph the spec presents — benchmarking the cold graph would credit ~97% savings on a workload that does not exist. CodeQL's 20-90 minute whole-program build reads all 8,000 files and has a structural 0% hit rate. And the true input set of a triage op is not enumerable without doing the analysis (a sanitizer three call-hops away), so a key that skips the model call is a correctness assertion in the worst possible domain to be silently wrong.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: The provider cache cannot cross the night — measured TTL cliff at 3,600s against a 24h nightly cadence — so for the ~18% of questions whose entire 16-28-artifact working set is unchanged, whole-chain replay avoids 100% of an already-84%-discounted cost, which is a larger marginal dollar figure than the spec's own '3-8%' claim by roughly 6x. verify_exec memoization (30-300s test runs, ~93% unchanged night to night) is a real latency win that appears nowhere on the bill.
ranked.why: Included in the ranking as the canonical HOSTILE shape, and it is the best-measured spec in the set (2,758 real transcripts, 21,012 model calls with provider usage counters attached, plus a live-probed baseline). Its value is diagnostic: it is where the Bazel analogy is most clearly wrong.
ranked.risk: The caterpillar has no partial-recompute frontier — every reason op consumes the whole transcript, so a changed file surfaced at step 3 invalidates the remaining 19 model calls where ~95% of tokens live, and the governing statistic is P(any artifact changed) = 62-82%/day (the critique argues ~82% once search targets are counted), not the 7% file rate. repo_pack hashes the whole tree and changes every ~10 minutes at 82 commits/day; the proposed merkle-sharding fix does not work while the 40k pack is still physically in every prompt. Agents read hot files at 2.45-4.25x repo-wide churn, so every naive estimate in this domain is wrong by an order of magnitude on P(any). Model non-determinism makes the transitive key compose over a value that is not reproducible — the deepest unsolved problem in applying Bazel semantics to model calls, and this is the workload where it bites hardest.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: 24h cadence versus ≤1h TTL, and reuse saves 100% of the 4,320 output tokens/run at the extraction layer which no prefix cache discounts. The one mechanism a review_id memo table structurally cannot do: Bazaarvoice syndicates 325M+ reviews to 1,250-1,750 retailer sites, so the same review text carries a different review_id at each — content-hash keying extracts it once across tenants.
ranked.why: Append-only immutable reviews with a measured 0.11% daily change rate (triangulated within 6% from two independent sources), and 97.8% of ops in two fan-in-1 leaf layers with no cross-talk. On paper this is the most reuse-friendly workload in the set.
ranked.risk: And it is the sharpest measured refutation of 'low change rate implies high value.' The spec's own arithmetic: the tuned baseline puts nightly incremental extraction at $0.14 — 'a reuse layer competing on the extraction layer is competing for fourteen cents a night.' The competition is not no-caching, it is a review_aspects table keyed on review_id plus Wayfair's published 10%-new-reviews retrigger rule, already shipped, in SQL. correlate/rollup amplification means ~6 new fingerprints spread across all 22 product classes so 100% of the rollup layer recomputes off 0.11% input change. Packing 25 reviews per call is a 6x win that beats caching outright and collapses reuse granularity 25x. The 14 fetch roots carry advancing watermark cursors that invalidate all 1.31M descendants nightly unless the customer refactors — and a system that requires the refactor is competing with the refactor.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Narrow but genuine: the 468 policy_compile ops run on PUBLIC payer PDFs and are identical for every payer, TPA, provider RCM vendor and UM vendor in the country — cross-tenant reuse that org-isolated provider caches cannot serve. The regression/drift suite (now near-mandatory under state AI-in-utilization-review statutes) re-runs frozen claims where prefix caching still bills 10% of input and 100% of ~20k output tokens per run.
ranked.why: Two independent roots, one frozen. The policy-corpus change rate is the best primary-source measurement in the batch — seven consecutive UHC bulletins parsed and counted at 18.7 revisions/month against a ~450-500 policy library, with a wrong prior publicly corrected mid-analysis.
ranked.risk: 96-100% of claim artifacts are new every run by construction, and ~97% of model ops carry a claim content hash, so nightly reuse is essentially zero — the value is confined to policy-change replay and eval replay, which are rare and (for eval replay) are triggered by changing the prompt or model, i.e. the key itself. Compiled criteria are already memoized in Postgres in every real deployment. Fan-out variance is correlated the wrong way: revisions concentrate in the highest-traffic policies. PHI blocks cross-tenant on everything except the public policy layer. And several states require adverse determinations to be made by a licensed reviewer on the current record, likely removing the ~28% of claims that run the token-heaviest rationale_and_letter path. The spec also never prices its own run (~$790/night, ~$0.40/claim against a $10-40M/yr labor line), which is the number that decides materiality.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Prefix caching is a discount on model input tokens and cannot touch a tool op — but 64% of this graph is deterministic tool work sitting entirely UPSTREAM of every model call, including hosted OCR, which is billed per page and dominates end-to-end latency. On a schema/prompt backfill, every fetch/rasterize/OCR key is unchanged (those layers never read the prompt) while every model key changes, so a 100k-document backfill re-executes 400k model calls and zero of 340k OCR ops.
ranked.why: The reuse layer's honest pitch here is 'your backfills become nearly free and much faster,' not 'your token bill falls' — and that is a real, orthogonal, provider-unreachable claim.
ranked.risk: 98.7% of input artifacts are documents never seen before — this is definitional for an invoice stream — so the store serves ~290 of 19,891 ops in the dominant nightly regime, and writing 19,891 keys to serve 290 hits is plausibly net-negative. (One upward correction: the spec undercounts its own 14% exception loop, where a human corrects one field and validate/match/code re-execute over unchanged OCR — 252 documents a night, not 23.) Everything else rests on replay frequency, which is entirely invented after a failed search, and the spec states outright that the conclusion flips between weekly and quarterly. Hosted OCR is a versioned remote service with no pinned version exposed, so its output is NOT a pure function of its inputs. Cross-tenant is a non-starter (counterparty PII, bank details, contractually confidential pricing), and GDPR erasure against a content-addressed store has no delete-descendants mechanism.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Prefix caching makes it cheaper to RE-SEND a telemetry result, never cheaper to RE-EXECUTE the Datadog query — so the 168-op telemetry sweep, which burns metered observability quota and 30-120s of wall clock, is entirely outside the provider mechanism. For postmortem re-runs and nightly vendor eval replay over 300 frozen incidents, the underlying windows are immutable and the sweep is free from a store, turning an API-throttled multi-hour eval into minutes.
ranked.why: Real but narrow, and it is a tool-memoization story rather than a dependency-tracking story — it does not need transitive keying through model outputs, and eval harnesses already hand-roll it as VCR/fixture caching.
ranked.risk: Wrong-end stability, which is a property of the domain rather than a tuning failure: the stable artifacts (runbooks, catalog, dashboards) are read by 8 cheap tool ops at depth 2, while always-changing telemetry is read at depth 4 upstream of every one of the 24 model ops. In the dominant mode (~70% of production runs: a new firing of a recurring alert) every byte of telemetry is new. The 9 PromQL and 3 log queries are over [now-15m] against a live TSDB, so their keys can never repeat and they sit directly upstream of the expensive layer. Re-runs inside a live incident are minutes apart — exactly the window the 1h tier already owns for free, and now the 24h tier too. Serving a cached telemetry result for a still-open window during a live incident is a correctness failure, not a cost regression.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Only two slices survive: output tokens (4,320/run at the normalize layer, ~1.24M/day/tenant, undiscounted by any prefix cache), and cross-tenant fingerprint sharing — KubePodCrashLooping / CPUThrottlingHigh normalize identically for every Prometheus shop on earth, and a multi-tenant store gets denser with each tenant added.
ranked.why: The 5-minute cadence with 50% structural window overlap and a Pareto fingerprint distribution looks maximally favorable at first glance, which is exactly why it is worth stating that it is not.
ranked.risk: The fan-in kills everything below depth 3: correlate_cluster consumes all 24 alert_normalize outputs and ~6 genuinely new fingerprints arrive per window, so its key changes essentially every run and the 57,000-token incident_triage layer recomputes unconditionally. The 12 metric/log queries are over [now-15m] and can never repeat. The baseline arithmetic is also broken in a way that inverts the conclusion — cached prefixes are billed once per run rather than once per request, so the stated 'tuned' baseline is ~2x WORSE than no caching and the hoisting move (170k cached tokens at 0.1x = 17k effective per call versus ~9k retrieved at full rate) roughly doubles the L5 bill. Every reuse figure derived from it must be discarded. And the entire surface is alert_normalize, 24 of 29 model ops, which a real triage service most likely handles with Alertmanager grouping and fingerprint rules rather than one LLM call per alert. Critique verdict: unusable as written.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Release cadence of 7-30 days is 200-700x the maximum TTL, so provider caching contributes literally nothing across runs — and yet the marginal saving is still near zero, which is the finding. The only real slices are within-release repetition (the same spec pair reviewed on the feature PR, the release branch, and at tag time, 3-5x per release, hours to days apart) and cross-customer prose-semantics on public vendor spec pairs, 20 of 79 model ops.
ranked.why: Recommended as a benchmark family precisely because it should return near zero, and its numbers are the only ones a critic independently reproduced by re-running the spec's own scripts against vendored real specs.
ranked.risk: The reuse layer's competitor here already ran: oasdiff is a deterministic differ inside the pipeline that scopes the model fan-out to the 24 changed operations before any model call, so by construction ~100% of layer 3/5/6 keys are new every run. The incremental-computation win was claimed for free, in CI, by a tool the customer already has. Hub-schema closure makes it worse: every Stripe operation directly references `error`, whose transitive closure covers a median 865 of 1,440 schemas, so a sound transitive key marks 100% of operations dirty on every release (measured: pct_ops_transitive = 100.0 on 10 of 11 real release pairs). The usage manifest is a rolling counter feeding 51 of 79 model ops and changes every run. Whole run is ~522k input tokens, weekly-to-monthly — single-digit dollars per customer even at 100% reuse.

ranked.headroom_over_provider_cache: Essentially none on the honest key. The one structurally provider-unreachable mechanism is real but thin: a flaky signature first triaged on Alice's PR at 09:14 served to Bob's unrelated PR at 16:40 is a 7-hour gap across two conversations with no shared prefix — impossible for prefix caching at any tier. That is the whole defensible case.
ranked.why: Included as the explicit negative control the suite needs. A workload where the honest answer is zero is evidence, and this one is unusually well sourced (SAP HANA's 102,529→16,345 symptom collapse at 76% recall / 96% precision, Google's 84% pass→fail flakiness, Apache's 4-hour median relatedness investigation).
ranked.risk: Every operation in this graph descends from a head_sha that is new on 100% of runs; A1 (run metadata), A4 (the diff) and A2 (the JUnit result set) are all depth-1 or -2 roots that change every time, so faithful Bazel/Nix key composition returns EXACTLY zero hits, not low hits. Every hit requires deliberately dropping real inputs from the key — the spec's own words: 'a heuristic matcher wearing a content-addressing costume.' Novelty also concentrates in the expensive region: layer D is 78% of tokens and fires only on new_regression clusters, i.e. failures whose diff has never existed before, so 78% of the bill has a structural reuse ceiling of ~zero. And the whole benefit is available today from a SELECT against a flake registry — that is BuildSheriff, and it is what Trunk and Datadog CI Visibility ship. The published 46% change rate should be deleted; the load-bearing number is 100%.

rationale:
INTERPRETATION. `expected_cost_weighted_reuse_pct` is the expected percentage reduction in DOLLARS versus a baseline that already has (a) tuned prefix caching — volatility-ordered blocks, correct breakpoint placement, floor-clearing prefixes, warm-one-then-fan-out, correct TTL tier — and (b) the Batch API where the run is latency-insensitive, blended over each domain's realistic mix of repeat triggers. Not raw hit rate, and not measured against an uncached counterfactual.

FIVE ADJUSTMENTS APPLIED ACROSS THE BOARD, all from the critiques.
1) BATCH API MISSING FROM FOUR BASELINES. contract-clauses, compliance-mapping, financial-close and claims-triage all describe canonical latency-insensitive nightly/monthly jobs and omit the flat 50% discount that composes with caching. Their stated baselines are ~2x too expensive, which doubles the apparent pot. I halved the residual before ranking. Three specs also price a 1h-tier write at 1.25x when it is 2x.
2) FREE INCUMBENTS. Nearly every domain already ships a coarse hand-rolled version: translation memory (30 years old, content-addressed, cross-project), SARIF partialFingerprints plus Semgrep's persisted triage state (which reduces the security-scan warm graph from 1,602 model ops to 5-50), `git diff --name-only HEAD@{1}` (testgen, docs-freshness), the candidate_requisition_score table, the review_aspects table plus a 10%-retrigger rule, BlackLine auto-certification clearing 58% of accounts, a SELECT against a flake registry, and a 20-line JSON sidecar for migrations. The layer's honest claim everywhere reduces to finer-than-artifact granularity plus cross-tenant sharing — the smaller and harder half. security-scan and ci-triage took the largest downgrades on this.
3) AMPLIFICATION. Low leaf churn does not imply high operation reuse, and the amplifier is a property of the customer's pipeline, not the domain: batching (1.1% → 24.1% at batch=25 in localization), blocking-shard granularity (2.5% → 33% at 512 shards in listings), churn/documentation-density correlation (6x measured in docs-freshness), agent hotness (2.45-4.25x in codebase-qa), and service-level whole-tree reads (2% → 60-80% in dependency-upgrade). Every spec that reported a friendly leaf rate got haircut by its own amplifier.
4) GLOBAL REDUCTION NODES. compliance-mapping's index_build (fan-in 744), listings' L6b (fan-in 512), testgen's coverage_parse and codebase-qa's repo_pack each convert a sub-1% input change into 100% invalidation under the STATED transitive rule. Fixing it means either weakening the key (a soundness bet) or asking the customer to restructure their pipeline — and a layer that requires the refactor is competing with the refactor. I priced these at the pessimistic end where the fix is a customer rewrite.
5) BASELINE ARITHMETIC ERRORS THAT INVERT CONCLUSIONS. alert-triage bills cached prefixes once per run rather than once per request, making its 'tuned' baseline ~2x worse than no caching and rendering all its reuse figures artifacts (critique verdict: unusable). docs-freshness applies an input-side multiplier to total cost (0.46x should be ~0.71x; output is 47% of that run). iac-drift double-counts its discount and understates tuned dollars ~3.5x. literature-screening's op table sums to 13,874 not 9,774, dropping its headline wide-layer share from 94% to 59%. Two errors ran the other way and I corrected upward: codebase-qa understates its own marginal dollars ~6x (whole-chain replay avoids 100% of an already-discounted cost), and invoice-extraction ignores its own 14% exception loop.

WHAT ACTUALLY DRIVES THE RANKING. Three properties separate the top from the bottom, and none of them is 'low change rate.' First, ARTIFACT IMMUTABILITY BY CONSTRUCTION — executed contracts, submitted resumes, signed clinical notes, published reviews are append-only by law or by system design, which is a categorically better foundation than any churn survey and is why contract-clauses, candidate-screening and medical-coding rank where they do. Second, CADENCE VERSUS TTL, which has just become a moving target: OpenAI shipped a 24h retention tier at zero premium and made it the default in May 2026, so any cadence under a day now has a shrinking moat (this hits financial-close's 40-minute-to-4-hour intra-close re-runs and every per-PR arm hardest), while Google's unbounded explicit cache is rented at $0.50-4.50/MTok/hour — roughly 18-96x underwater on a 24h gap — so it is a short-horizon tool in a long-horizon interface. Monthly and annual cadences (contract-clauses, literature-screening) are the only ones structurally safe from provider TTL extension. Third, WHAT THE PROVIDER CANNOT TOUCH AT ALL: output tokens (64% of tuned cost in localization, 68% of residual in candidate-screening, 47% in docs-freshness), tool ops (hosted OCR at $0.01-0.05/page in invoice and contracts, 860 pytest runs in testgen, 168 metered observability queries in log-rca), concurrent fan-out (measured: 5 of 5 callers billed cache_creation at 0ms skew, so a store with in-flight dedup wins regardless of TTL), and cross-tenant identity on public artifacts (payer policy PDFs, vendor SOC 2s, public module version pairs) which org-isolated provider caches can never serve.

TWO BLIND SPOTS SHARED BY ALL 24 SPECS, which I treated as a uniform additional haircut. NOBODY PRICES THE STORE: at these op counts (9,109 artifacts x 30 runs in security-scan, 42,516 ops/run in listings, 3.25M keys/run in catalog) hashing, storage and lookup are request-priced not storage-priced (~$74-217/month at 100M ops, with retention nearly free), and against domains concluding a $1.50-per-run marginal, store overhead could consume the entire margin invisibly. AND MODEL NON-DETERMINISM BREAKS TRANSITIVE COMPOSITION: only codebase-qa and api-migration take it seriously. If a model op's output hash is not stable, every one of these graphs collapses to 'reuse the whole run or nothing.' That should be measured once, cheaply, before any of these benchmarks is built.

FAMILY SELECTION. Shape coverage: deep chain (codebase-qa, max_depth 45, cumulative fan-in), wide independent (contract-clauses), layered DAG (compliance-mapping, api-contract-diff), and — a shape the brief did not name but which the corpus contains and which I think matters — a RELATIONAL middle with pairwise coupling and a global stitch (listings). financial-close adds a fifth axis: a flat band re-run hours apart, which is the direct test of whether a 24h provider tier eats the layer. contract-clauses is the most favourable case, so a negative there is strong evidence against the whole thesis and a positive locates the beachhead on the long-cadence, immutable-artifact, wide-independent end. api-contract-diff is included as harness calibration rather than as a candidate: its numbers were independently reproduced, and the free deterministic differ already claims the incremental-computation win, so if the harness reports a large saving there the harness is wrong. I dropped localization (highest-quality change-rate measurement in the set, but listings already carries the batch-size sweep and TM makes its incumbent test hard to read) and etl-validation (its likely dominant competitor — gate the model call on non-nominal signal — is missing from its own baseline).

MANDATORY ARMS FOR WHICHEVER FAMILIES RUN. (1) Three arms, not two: tuned prefix cache + Batch, tuned PLUS the customer's existing hand-rolled memo/dirty-bit, and the reuse store. Arm two is the real hurdle. (2) Sweep batch size — prefix economics push it up, reuse economics push it down, and fixing it measures an arbitrary point. (3) Report both keying regimes (raw-artifact versus projection/field-scoped) — listings' FEED_NOISE knob and compliance-mapping's pairwise-versus-transitive choice each swing their result by 20-80 points. (4) Reuse-correctness gates must compare served output against the RECORDED populating-run output, never against a fresh recompute; four specs get this right and three specify byte-identity gates that are vacuous for served ops and unpassable for recomputed ones. (5) Under-invalidation must be a hard failure, and staleness bounds should be priced: a 1%/95% bound costs ~299 recomputes per operation class per validity window, which at low hit volume means the shadow rate approaches 1 and the audit is unaffordable — relevant to iac-drift, claims-triage and medical-coding, where staleness is a compliance event rather than a cost regression.
